title: How the Internet Works
subtitle: The internet is just computers passing notes
objectives: Explain what actually happens when you open a website
Describe how packets, IP addresses, and DNS get data to the right place
Trace a request from your browser to a server and back
Tell the difference between TCP and UDP and when each is used

exercises.prompt: You open a website. Roughly how many separate computers might your request pass through before it reaches the server?
exercises.why: Your data hops through many routers along the way — often 10 to 20 — each one passing it one step closer to the destination.
exercises.goDeeper: Run `traceroute google.com` (or `tracert` on Windows) and you'll literally see every hop your packets take across the internet.

exercises.prompt: Data doesn't travel as one big blob. It's broken into small chunks called ______.
exercises.why: The internet splits your data into small packets, sends them independently, and reassembles them at the other end.
exercises.goDeeper: Packets can take *different routes* and arrive out of order. Something has to put them back in order — that's TCP's job, coming up in lesson 4.

exercises.prompt: Every device on the internet needs one of these to be found. What is it?
exercises.why: An IP address (like 142.250.72.14) is a device's location on the internet — data can't be delivered without one.
exercises.goDeeper: There aren't enough of the old IPv4 addresses (~4.3 billion) for the world, which is why IPv6 exists with 340 undecillion addresses — enough for every grain of sand to have trillions.

exercises.prompt: Match each piece to what it does.

pairs.right: A small chunk of your data
A device's location on the internet

exercises.why: Packets carry the data, IP addresses say where it's going, and routers move it hop by hop.
exercises.goDeeper: Routers don't know the whole path to the destination — each one just knows the *next best hop*. The internet has no central map.

exercises.prompt: There's no master computer running the internet. So how do packets find their way?
choices: A central server in the US decides every route
Each router just forwards to the next-best hop toward the target
Packets are sent to every computer until one matches
Your ISP pre-computes the full path
exercises.why: The internet is decentralized. Each router makes a local decision — 'who gets me closer?' — and no single machine is in charge.
exercises.goDeeper: This decentralization is why the internet is so resilient: knock out a router and traffic just routes around it. It was literally a design goal from its Cold-War-era origins.

exercises.prompt: You type `google.com`, but computers route by IP address. Who turns the name into the number?
exercises.why: DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's phonebook — it looks up the name 'google.com' and returns its IP address.
exercises.goDeeper: Humans remember names; machines need numbers. DNS is the translation layer that lets us live in a world of words.

exercises.prompt: DNS translates a human-friendly ______ into a machine-friendly IP address.
exercises.why: A domain name like 'netflix.com' is for humans; DNS converts it to the IP address machines actually use.

exercises.prompt: Put a DNS lookup in order (simplified).
steps: Browser asks: what's the IP for example.com?
Check the local cache — seen it recently?
If not cached, ask a DNS resolver
exercises.why: DNS checks the fastest sources first (local cache) before asking a resolver, then hands the browser an IP to connect to.
exercises.goDeeper: Results are cached at many levels (browser, OS, resolver) with a 'TTL' — time to live. That's why a DNS change can take hours to reach everyone.

exercises.prompt: In October 2016, a company called Dyn was attacked. Suddenly Twitter, Spotify, Reddit, and Netflix all went dark at once — even though those companies were fine. What had been knocked out?
exercises.why: Dyn was a big DNS provider. Take out DNS and users can't translate names to IPs — so the sites become unreachable even though they're running perfectly.
exercises.goDeeper: DNS is a quiet single point of failure for huge chunks of the web. This is why serious systems use multiple DNS providers.

exercises.prompt: Why does DNS cache results instead of looking up every time? Select all that apply.
choices: Lookups take time — caching makes pages load faster
It reduces load on DNS servers
It makes the answer more accurate
The same names are requested over and over
exercises.why: Caching is about speed and load: popular names are requested constantly, so remembering the answer avoids a repeat round-trip. It does NOT make answers more accurate — stale caches can even serve outdated IPs.
exercises.goDeeper: This is your first taste of caching — a theme you'll see everywhere in system design. Keep the hot answer close.

exercises.prompt: Before your browser can send an HTTP request to a server, what does it need first?
exercises.why: You can't send data anywhere without a destination address. DNS supplies the server's IP first — then the request can travel.

exercises.prompt: Order what happens when you visit `example.com`.
steps: DNS resolves example.com to an IP address
Browser opens a connection to that IP
Server sends back an HTTP response
exercises.why: Every web page load is this dance: name → IP → connect → ask → process → answer → render.
exercises.goDeeper: On a real HTTPS site there's also a TLS handshake after connecting, which encrypts everything. That's why 'https' has the 's' — secure.

exercises.prompt: Place the missing piece: your browser needs to turn 'example.com' into an IP before reaching the server.
exercises.why: DNS sits between you and the server on that first step, translating the name so your browser knows where to connect.

exercises.prompt: Light travels fast, but not instantly. A round trip from New York to a server in London and back is roughly how many milliseconds — at the physical minimum?
exercises.why: Even at the speed of light through fiber, NY↔London round-trips take ~70ms. Physics sets a floor on latency that no amount of engineering can beat.
exercises.goDeeper: This is why companies put servers *close to users* (that's what CDNs do, a later unit). You can't outrun the speed of light — so you shorten the distance.

exercises.prompt: Your page felt slow. The server responded in 5ms, but the total was 300ms. Where did the time most likely go?
exercises.why: If the server itself only took 5ms, the other 295ms was the network — the round-trips of getting data there and back. Distance and hops cost time.
exercises.goDeeper: A rule of thumb: often the *network*, not the server, is your latency bottleneck. Measure before you optimize.

lessons.title: TCP vs UDP: reliable vs fast

exercises.prompt: You're loading a bank statement. Every byte must arrive, in order, no errors. Which protocol fits?
exercises.why: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) guarantees delivery and order — it re-sends lost packets and reassembles them correctly. Perfect for data you can't afford to lose.
exercises.goDeeper: TCP does this with acknowledgements: the receiver confirms each chunk, and anything unconfirmed gets re-sent. Reliability has a cost — extra round-trips.

exercises.prompt: You're on a live video call. A dropped frame is fine, but a 2-second delay to re-send it is not. Which protocol fits?
exercises.why: UDP (User Datagram Protocol) just fires packets and doesn't wait for confirmation. For live audio/video, a missing frame is better than a laggy one — speed beats perfection.
exercises.goDeeper: This is a classic tradeoff: reliability vs latency. You'll make this call again and again in system design.

exercises.prompt: Match the use case to the better protocol.
exercises.why: TCP for anything that must be complete and correct; UDP for small or real-time traffic where speed matters more than perfection.
exercises.goDeeper: DNS traditionally uses UDP because a lookup is tiny and fast — if it's lost, just ask again. Modern DNS-over-HTTPS uses TCP for privacy.

exercises.prompt: You're designing a multiplayer game's networking. Slide toward what you'd prioritize for player-movement updates.
exercises.why: For fast-moving player positions, low latency wins — a slightly stale position that arrives NOW beats a perfect one that arrives late. Most competitive games lean UDP.
exercises.goDeeper: Real games send *newer* position updates constantly, so a lost one is instantly replaced. Re-sending old positions (TCP) would actually make gameplay feel worse.

exercises.prompt: The core tradeoff between TCP and UDP: TCP gives you reliability, UDP gives you ______.
exercises.why: TCP trades speed for guaranteed, ordered delivery. UDP trades those guarantees for raw speed and low latency.
exercises.goDeeper: Neither is 'better' — the right choice depends entirely on what your system values most. That judgment IS system design.

exercises.prompt: You've now traced a request end to end. Which statement best captures how the internet moves your data?
choices: One connection sends the whole file at once with no addressing
Data is split into packets, addressed by IP, routed hop-by-hop, and reassembled
A central server copies data directly to your screen
The browser stores everything locally and never contacts a server
exercises.why: That's the whole picture: split into packets, addressed with IPs (found via DNS), routed hop-by-hop by routers, and reassembled — reliably with TCP or fast with UDP.
exercises.goDeeper: Everything else in this course — caching, load balancing, databases — is built on top of this foundation. You now understand the ground floor.
